observation.visible_scene: A macro close-up of a single faceted, pale yellow-green diamond (or similar transparent gemstone) resting on a smooth, dark-gray reflective surface. A clear mirror-image reflection of the stone appears directly below it, and the background is a featureless gray gradient. The stone stays centered in frame throughout the excerpt.
visible_changes: The gemstone's orientation changes gradually and continuously across the clip: the broad, bright table facet that initially faces the viewer from the upper-left turns progressively edge-on, while the crown and pavilion facets on the right side of the stone rotate into view. By the last frame the table reads as a narrow bright strip on the left and the right-hand facets dominate the silhouette.

Colored dispersion flashes migrate across the facets as the viewing geometry shifts: a violet/purple flash at the lower edge early on becomes a blue flash (mid-clip), then a cyan/green flash, while a magenta/purple edge appears on the right side in the later frames.
The mirror reflection below tracks these same changes in orientation and flash color, confirming the reflection belongs to the rotating stone rather than being a separate object.
The stone's position in the frame and its contact point with the surface remain essentially fixed; the change is rotational, not translational, and no part of the stone leaves or enters the frame.
No editing cut is visible; the motion reads as continuous within the excerpt.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the rotation is the stone turning on a turntable or the camera orbiting the stone cannot be resolved from this segment alone (the background is featureless).
The full extent of the spin, the light-source arrangement, and what happens before t=0 or after t=1.6s are outside the crop.
uncertain_details: Exact rotation direction and whether the apparent motion is object rotation versus camera orbit are indistinguishable here.
The hue sequence of the dispersion flashes (violet→blue→cyan/green, plus magenta on the right) is approximate and depends on lighting not fully visible.
Minor dust specks in the background may shift slightly, but this is too faint to attribute confidently to camera motion.

the excerpt form a complete story. Missing context outside this segment stays unknown.

do not invent a smooth transition or a causal mechanism to connect the two views.

properties. Cover the main visible process, not just scenery. Distinguish object movement from
camera movement, reflection from separate objects, expansion from translation, deformation from
occlusion, and an already ongoing process from its onset. Only state what the clip supports;

and their relative positions before describing motion. Treat camera motion as uncertain when the
background evidence is insufficient, and retain clear relative changes despite that uncertainty.
